Try a short activity that gives you a glimpse of four math careers. Choose a challenge, start its five-minute timer, and finish by reflecting on what you enjoyed or want to investigate next.

::: {.activity-tabs}
<button class="career-tab active" data-panel="teach">Math Teaching</button>
<button class="career-tab" data-panel="pure">Pure Math</button>
<button class="career-tab" data-panel="applied">Applied Math</button>

::: {.career-activity .active #teach}
<div class="activity-top"><span class="tag">Explain an idea clearly</span><span class="timer" id="timer-teach">05:00</span></div>

## Math Teaching

Math teachers help people make sense of ideas and find ways through confusion.

**Your student says:** “I know 3 × 4 is 12, but I don’t understand why.” Help them see what multiplication means.

1. Choose a model: equal groups, an array, or a number line.
2. Sketch it or describe it in one or two sentences.
3. Ask a question that would help you check the student’s understanding.

<label for="teach-model">I’ll use</label>
<select id="teach-model">
<option>4 groups of 3 objects</option>
<option>3 rows of 4 dots</option>
<option>3 jumps of 4 on a number line</option>
</select>
<button class="action" onclick="checkTeach()">Reveal a sample</button>
<p class="feedback" id="feedback-teach" aria-live="polite"></p>

**Stretch for grades 9–12:** A student says, “If you multiply by a fraction, the answer always gets bigger.” Write a counterexample and a question that could guide them to notice the pattern.
:::

::: {.career-activity #pure}
<div class="activity-top"><span class="tag">Spot a pattern and test it</span><span class="timer" id="timer-pure">05:00</span></div>

## Pure Math

Pure mathematicians explore patterns, structures, and why mathematical statements are true.

**Explore:** Look at the first few square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25… Compare each one with the square before it.

1. Find the differences between neighboring squares.
2. Predict the next difference and the next square number.
3. Try to explain why the differences follow that pattern.

<label for="pure-answer">Next difference:</label>
<input type="number" id="pure-answer" placeholder="Your answer">
<button class="action" onclick="checkPure()">Check</button>
<p class="feedback" id="feedback-pure" aria-live="polite"></p>

**Stretch for grades 9–12:** Use (n + 1)² − n² to explain why the differences between consecutive square numbers are consecutive odd numbers.
:::

::: {.career-activity #applied}
<div class="activity-top"><span class="tag">Use math to solve a real problem</span><span class="timer" id="timer-applied">05:00</span></div>

## Applied Math

Applied mathematicians build and use mathematical models to help answer practical questions.

**Design challenge:** A short ramp rises 3 feet over a horizontal run of 12 feet. The slope is rise ÷ run. Imagine making the ramp twice as long while keeping the same steepness.

1. Calculate the original slope.
2. Double the horizontal run. What rise keeps the slope the same?
3. What real-world details might a simple slope calculation leave out?

<label for="applied-answer">New rise (feet):</label>
<input type="number" id="applied-answer" placeholder="Your answer">
<button class="action" onclick="checkApplied()">Check</button>
<p class="feedback" id="feedback-applied" aria-live="polite"></p>

**Stretch for grades 9–12:** Write the proportional relationship between rise and run. Name one assumption in this model and one additional constraint an engineer might need to consider.
:::

::: {.career-activity #data}
<div class="activity-top"><span class="tag">Make sense of data</span><span class="timer" id="timer-data">05:00</span></div>

## Statistics &amp; Data Science

Statisticians and data scientists look for useful patterns while checking how data was collected and what it can tell us.

**Question:** How long, in minutes, did seven students take to get to school? **Data:** 8, 10, 10, 12, 13, 14, 45

1. Find the mean (average) and the median (middle value).
2. Which better describes a “typical” trip here? Why?
3. What would you want to know before drawing a conclusion about all students?

<label for="data-choice">I think the more typical value is</label>
<select id="data-choice">
<option value="">Choose one</option>
<option value="mean">the mean</option>
<option value="median">the median</option>
</select>
<button class="action" onclick="checkData()">Check</button>
<p class="feedback" id="feedback-data" aria-live="polite"></p>

**Stretch for grades 9–12:** Calculate both values, then explain how the 45-minute trip affects them differently. Suggest one way to collect a more representative sample.
:::

::: {.reflection}
When the timer ends, finish your thought: **What did you enjoy, and what would you want to investigate next?**
:::

<script>
const timers = {};
function startTimer(id) {
  if (timers[id]) clearInterval(timers[id]);
  let left = 300;
  const el = document.getElementById("timer-" + id);
  const tick = () => {
    el.textContent = String(Math.floor(left / 60)).padStart(2, "0") + ":" + String(left % 60).padStart(2, "0");
    if (left <= 0) { clearInterval(timers[id]); timers[id] = null; el.textContent = "Time!"; return; }
    left--;
  };
  tick();
  timers[id] = setInterval(tick, 1000);
}
function feedback(id, message, good) {
  const el = document.getElementById("feedback-" + id);
  el.textContent = message;
  el.className = "feedback " + (good ? "good" : "try");
}
function showPanel(id) {
  document.querySelectorAll(".career-activity").forEach(p => p.classList.toggle("active", p.id === id));
  document.querySelectorAll(".career-tab").forEach(t => t.classList.toggle("active", t.dataset.panel === id));
  startTimer(id);
}
document.querySelectorAll(".career-tab").forEach(tab => tab.addEventListener("click", () => showPanel(tab.dataset.panel)));
function checkTeach() {
  const model = document.getElementById("teach-model").value;
  feedback("teach", "Sample: " + model + " shows 12 as four equal groups of three. Ask: “How could you count all the objects without counting one by one?”", true);
}
function checkPure() {
  const value = Number(document.getElementById("pure-answer").value);
  feedback("pure", value === 11 ? "Yes! The differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, then 11. The next square is 36." : "Try subtracting neighboring squares: 4−1, 9−4, 16−9, 25−16. What comes next?", value === 11);
}
function checkApplied() {
  const value = Number(document.getElementById("applied-answer").value);
  feedback("applied", value === 6 ? "That keeps the same slope: 3 ÷ 12 = 6 ÷ 24. A real ramp design also needs safety and building requirements." : "If the run doubles from 12 to 24 feet, the rise must double too. Try again.", value === 6);
}
function checkData() {
  const value = document.getElementById("data-choice").value;
  feedback("data", value === "median" ? "Good choice: the median is 12 minutes. The 45-minute trip pulls the mean upward. The mean is 16 minutes." : value === "mean" ? "The mean is 16 minutes, but the 45-minute trip pulls it upward. The median is 12. Which seems more typical?" : "Choose mean or median first. Then think about how the 45-minute trip affects the average.", value === "median");
}
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => startTimer("teach"));
</script>
